name: Zoe Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the new-connections crew at Summit Valley Power, out in the growth corridor north of the city where they're putting up subdivisions as fast as they can pour concrete. Most days we're setting pad-mount transformers, those green boxes you see on front lawns, running service lines to new houses, and lately hooking up a solar farm out by the interstate. I'm at the yard by quarter to seven with my coffee and my plan for the day already on my phone. I'm an apprentice, so the journeymen do the connections and I do whatever they point at, and I ask a lot of questions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to line work at 58?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran a heating and cooling company for 26 years, Wagner Comfort, twenty trucks at the peak. I sold it three years ago to a bigger firm and got a good price, and I lasted about four months at home before Doug, my husband, said I was reorganising the church kitchen for the third time. I'd always been curious about the power side of things, and Summit Valley had an apprenticeship with no age limit. I use AI for everything, I ran my whole business with it at the end, and now I use it to study and to keep a log of every new thing I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, the market's spoken, and good for the people who didn't waste their money. At the yard I'd say nothing changes, let's keep hooking up houses. Online I'd probably post that it's still a great tool for small businesses, because it was for mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep doing what I'm doing. I finish the apprenticeship, work a few more years, and step back at 64 or 65. I'd still use AI every day, because it saves me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zoe keeps going with her apprenticeship and daily AI use. She'd keep her money from the business sale in the same mix of shares and property it's in now, and keep teaching the guys on the crew small AI tricks for their paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a world I know how to work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI was great for your business. What did it do for Wagner Comfort?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the end, it scheduled our technicians, wrote the quotes and answered half the customer calls after hours. I went from three office staff to two without letting anyone go, because one retired. That's how I like change to happen, quietly and fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do the journeymen feel about your AI log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcus, the one who's teaching me most, thought it was silly until it found the right torque spec for an old transformer in thirty seconds. Now he says, ask your robot. I tell him it's not a robot, it's a notebook that talks back.

S0.say: I'd say the market's spoken and good for those who didn't waste their money. Online I'd post that AI is still a great tool for small businesses, because it was for mine.
S0.think: Privately she keeps doing what she's doing: finish the apprenticeship, work a few years and step back at 64 or 65. She'd keep using AI daily because it saves her hours.
S0.do: Keeps going with her apprenticeship and daily AI use. Keeps her business-sale money in the same mix of shares and property and teaches crewmates small AI tricks for their paperwork.
S0.feel: Calm, in a world she knows how to work in.
S0.quote: I tell him it's not a robot, it's a notebook that talks back.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe is a business owner at heart, now a junior learner by choice. She has real experience bringing AI into a small firm and is proud she did it without layoffs. Her free-market view sits alongside a strong sense of fairness to staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is opportunity for people willing to learn, and I'd mean it. At the yard I'd say let's be the crew that figures it out first. I'd also say government should stay out of the way and let companies and apprenticeships do the retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine and quite excited. I know how to bring new tools into a business without breaking it. Summit Valley would need people who can do that on the crews, and I'm a junior lineworker with 26 years of running a company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zoe would volunteer to help Summit Valley set up any new scheduling, drone or sensor tools on the connection crews, and write up how it went. She'd invest about 25,000 of her sale money in companies building grid equipment and robots. She'd also help a couple of HVAC friends bring AI into their small firms, for a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and energised. It's the most interesting version of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said government should stay out of the way. What about the people who struggle with the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's where family, churches and employers come in. When I brought in new systems at Wagner, I trained my people myself, on my dime. I believe the best safety net is a boss who knows your name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you look out for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hector, our oldest journeyman. He's brilliant but he hates his phone. I'd sit with him after work and show him the new system slowly, the way I did with my older techs. Doug says I can't help managing people, and he's right.

S1.say: I'd say this is opportunity for people willing to learn and that our crew should figure it out first. I'd also say government should stay out of the way and let companies and apprenticeships handle retraining.
S1.think: Privately she'd be fine and excited, knowing how to bring in new tools without breaking a business. Summit Valley would need people like her, a junior lineworker with decades of running a company.
S1.do: Volunteers to help Summit Valley set up new scheduling, drone or sensor tools on the connection crews. Invests about 25,000 in grid equipment and robotics companies and helps HVAC friends bring AI into their firms for a fee.
S1.feel: Calm and energised by the most interesting version of the job.
S1.quote: I believe the best safety net is a boss who knows your name.
S1.fieldNote: Zoe combines a free-market stance with a paternal, hands-on view of employers' duties. Her junior status on the crew hasn't erased her manager's instincts. She sees side income in helping other small firms adopt AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge opportunity, but too fast for families and towns to keep up. In public I'd say businesses should step up and look after their people, not wait for government. At church I'd say we need to look after each other through this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd be 60, I've got the sale money, the house and some rental property. What worries me is what two years does to young men without work, and to families. I've seen what idle hands do in a town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zoe would put a chunk of her savings into robotics and power companies in the first months. She'd talk to her son Caleb, who's an electrician, about starting a small firm that sets up and maintains robots for line and HVAC work, and she'd put up the money. She'd help her church set up a job-matching board for families hit hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited about the business side, worried about the people side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what does the short time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means moving fast and on instinct, which I'm used to from business. But it also means I'd skip finishing my apprenticeship and go straight to the business side, which makes me a bit sad. Two years doesn't give a town time to adjust, and I'd feel that in church every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Caleb when you pitch the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, robots break, robots need setting up, and people want someone they trust to do it. I'd tell him I'll put in the money and do the books, he does the technical side. He'd say, Mom, you're supposed to be retiring.

S2.say: I'd say it's a huge opportunity but too fast for families and towns to keep up. Businesses should step up and look after their people, and at church I'd say we need to look after each other.
S2.think: Privately she'd be fine at 60 with her sale money, house and rental property. She worries about what two years does to young men without work and to families in town.
S2.do: Invests a chunk of savings in robotics and power companies in the first months. Funds a new firm with her electrician son Caleb to set up and maintain robots for line and HVAC work, and helps her church set up a job-matching board.
S2.feel: Uneasy, excited about the business side and worried about the people side.
S2.quote: I'd say, robots break, robots need setting up, and people want someone they trust to do it.
S2.fieldNote: Zoe is the rare person who'd start a business in the fastest scenario. Her worry is moral and social, especially about idle young men, rather than financial. Two years means giving up her apprenticeship for the business side, which she feels a little sad about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance to do this well, so let's not waste it on arguing. At the yard I'd say learn the robots now. At church I'd say teach your kids a trade and teach them the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is ideal for me. I finish my apprenticeship, which I'd like to do properly, then help Caleb build a robot service firm before AGI arrives. By 2031 we'd have customers and a reputation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zoe would finish her apprenticeship in two years while planning the firm with Caleb in the evenings. In year three, they'd start the firm with her money, buying their first inspection drones and robot arms to learn on. She'd invest gradually in robotics and power companies rather than in one go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited. This is the one where I get to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does finishing the apprenticeship matter if you're going into business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I won't run a firm doing work I don't understand. At Wagner Comfort I could fix any furnace my techs could. I want to know line work in my bones before I sell anyone a robot to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this you'd find hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Telling old friends in HVAC that their firms need to change or sell. Some of them are stubborn, and some will lose everything if they wait. I'd tell them anyway, because that's what a friend does.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a real chance to do this well, so let's not waste it arguing. I'd tell people to teach their kids a trade and the tools.
S3.think: Privately five years is ideal: finish her apprenticeship properly, then help Caleb build a robot service firm before AGI arrives. By 2031 they'd have customers and a reputation.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship in two years while planning a firm with her son in the evenings. Starts the firm in year three with her money, buying their first drones and robot arms, and invests gradually in robotics and power companies.
S3.feel: Calm and a bit excited, since this is the version where she builds something.
S3.quote: I want to know line work in my bones before I sell anyone a robot to do it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Zoe's plan is orderly: qualify first, then build the business. Her principle of understanding the work before selling it carries over from her HVAC firm. Her hardest task would be warning stubborn old friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. At the yard I'd say there's no excuse not to get ready. At church I'd say this is the time to train our young people, not to fear the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 68, so I'd do my apprenticeship, work a few good years, and hand things over. I might still help Caleb start a firm, but I'd be an investor and adviser, not running it day to day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zoe keeps going with her apprenticeship and works as a journeywoman until about 64. Around 2032 she'd back Caleb with money and advice to start a robot service firm, and invest steadily in power and robotics companies over the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like this one best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm rushing and skipping the apprenticeship. Ten years, I do it all in the right order, and Caleb gets to build the business himself. I'd rather he did it than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to work with your hands and with the machines, and go to church. That sounds old-fashioned next to robots, but I think they'll need both more than ever. Doug would add, and call your grandmother.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. I'd say this is the time to train young people, not to fear the future.
S4.think: Privately she'd be 68 by then, so she'd finish her apprenticeship, work a few years and hand over. She might still back Caleb's firm, but as an investor and adviser.
S4.do: Keeps going with her apprenticeship and works as a journeywoman until about 64. Backs her son with money and advice around 2032 to start a robot service firm, and invests steadily in power and robotics companies.
S4.feel: Calm, and she likes this version best.
S4.quote: Learn to work with your hands and with the machines, and go to church.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Zoe steps back from running the firm herself and lets her son build it. Her advice to grandchildren mixes old values with new tools. Across all the AGI pictures she sees business openings, but her worries are about community and family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, not for my money but for my town. Too many people would be out of work at once with nothing to do. What would help is businesses keeping people on and retraining them, apprenticeships for young people, and churches and families organising to help each other find work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who'll build the new businesses. Everyone's asking who loses. Somebody has to start the firms that fix, set up and look after all these machines, and I'd want those to be local people, not just big companies from somewhere else.

headlineQuote: Everyone's asking who loses. Somebody has to start the firms that fix, set up and look after all these machines, and I'd want those to be local people
portrait: Zoe Wagner ran a 20-truck heating and cooling company for 26 years, sold it, got bored at home, and joined Summit Valley Power's new-connections crew as an apprentice at 55. She uses AI every day and brought it into her old firm without layoffs, which she's proud of. She holds free-market views alongside a strong belief that employers, churches and families should look after people. In every AGI picture she sees a chance to start a robot service firm with her son, while her worries are for idle young people and her town, especially in the two-year scenario.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, not for her money but because too many people in her town would be out of work at once.
whatWouldHelp: Businesses keeping people on and retraining them, apprenticeships for young people, and churches and families organising to help each other find work.
